title: Polymeric Sand vs Regular Sand for Pavers: Polymeric Wins
metaDescription: Polymeric sand keeps paver joints full 3-10 years vs topping up regular sand every 1-2, so it wins for most patios. Regular sand still wins in 4 cases.
h1: Polymeric Sand vs Regular Sand for Pavers: Which Is Better?
keywords: is all polymeric sand the same
what type of sand for pavers
polymeric sand vs mortar for paver joints
intro:
Polymeric sand beats regular sand for most paver patios, walkways and driveways, because its binder hardens the joint so it stays full for 3 to 10 years instead of needing a top-up every year or two. It also keeps out far more weeds and ants. Regular sand is cheaper and almost impossible to install badly, and it still wins in a handful of specific cases.

This comparison covers what each one does in a joint, which regular sand to use if you go that way, how they differ on weeds, drainage, movement, installation and cost over five years, and how to switch an old plain-sand patio over to polymeric joints.
quickAnswer: Choose polymeric sand for a paver patio, walkway or driveway on a stable base when you can install it in dry weather. Choose regular angular joint sand for a base that still moves, a temporary or casual surface, or when you cannot get two dry days. Use neither in permeable pavers, which need chip stone.

sections.heading: Polymeric Sand vs Regular Sand: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Factor | Regular joint sand | Polymeric sand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How it holds | Friction and gravity | Binder hardens when wet |
| Weed resistance | Poor | Good, not perfect |
| Ant resistance | Poor | Good |
| Washout in heavy rain | Common | Rare when installed correctly |
| Installation | Very easy, any weather | Moderate, needs dry pavers and forecast |
| Haze risk | None | Yes, if done poorly |
| Upkeep | Top up every 1 to 2 years | Refresh every 3 to 10 years |
| Material cost | Low | Several times higher |
| Permeable pavers | Not used; chip stone instead | Not suitable |

**Winner for most patios: polymeric sand.** It costs more and asks for a careful installation, but rewards it with joints that stay full and resist weeds for years. Regular sand is cheap and forgiving, but you will be sweeping in more sand and pulling weeds every season.

Most hardscape installers now finish concrete paver jobs with polymeric sand because callbacks for weeds and washed-out joints cost them more than the sand does. The people still weighing the choice are usually homeowners with an older plain-sand patio, and the switching steps are near the end of this page.

sections.heading: What Is the Difference Between Polymeric Sand and Regular Sand?
sections.body:
Both fill the gaps between pavers so the pavers lock together and do not shift. The difference is what keeps the sand in the joint.

### Regular sand

Regular joint sand is a graded, angular sand held in place by friction and gravity. It packs reasonably well, but rain, wind, hoses and foot traffic move it a little at a time. When the joint drops below the paver edge, pavers can shift, and the loose surface becomes a home for seeds and ants.

### Polymeric sand

Polymeric sand is a similar graded sand blended with a dry polymer binder. Water activates the binder, which coats the grains and glues them together as it dries. The joint ends up firm with a little flex, so it stays where you put it.

### Is play sand polymeric sand?

No. Play sand is plain, very fine, rounded sand with no binder. It is also a poor choice for paver joints of any kind, because rounded grains do not lock together and wash out quickly.

### Is all polymeric sand the same?

No. Products differ in the joint width they cover, how forgiving the binder is during watering, how much haze they tend to leave and how firm the joint sets. Fine paver sands and coarse wide-joint binders for flagstone are different products altogether. Our [best polymeric sand](/best-polymeric-sand/) roundup sorts them by joint width.

sections.heading: What Type of Regular Sand Should You Use for Pavers?
sections.body:
If you go with regular sand, the type matters. For paver joints, the usual choices are kiln-dried paver joint sand, fine concrete sand or a paver maker's own plain jointing sand. All are angular and pack reasonably well.

### Kiln-dried joint sand

Kiln-dried sand is the easiest to work with. It is completely dry and flows into narrow joints without clumping, which is why it is sold specifically as paver joint sand. Home centers commonly stock it in 50 lb bags.

### Concrete sand

Concrete sand is coarser and usually cheaper, and its angular grains lock together well. It has to be dry to sweep into narrow joints, so spread it out on a sunny day before you use it.

### Sands to avoid

Play sand and mason sand are both fine and rounded. They do not lock together, so they wash out quickly and make every weakness of regular sand worse.

### Joint sand vs bedding sand

The bedding sand under the pavers is a separate layer from the joint sand. Bedding is usually coarse concrete sand screeded to about an inch thick. This comparison is only about the joints. Polymeric sand should never be used as a bedding layer.

sections.heading: Which Is Better for Weeds, Ants and Washout?
sections.body:
Polymeric sand is better on all three, and these are the reasons most people consider it in the first place.

### Weeds

Loose sand becomes a seedbed once it collects a little organic debris, and weeds root deep into it. A hardened polymeric joint gives roots little to grip, so most of what grows is shallow and pulls out easily. Wind-blown seeds can still sprout in dust and leaves on top, so sweeping is still part of the routine.

### Ants

Ants dig easily through loose sand and push mounds up onto the pavers, and colonies can undermine the bedding layer over time. Polymeric joints are much harder to excavate, and owners commonly report far fewer mounds after switching. Ants can still get in through cracked joints or at patio edges.

### Washout

Heavy rain, especially from a downspout, flushes loose sand out of the joints. Correctly installed polymeric sand rarely washes out. An under-watered polymeric joint, though, can wash out almost as badly as plain sand, which is why the activation step matters.

### Weed killer is not a substitute

Spraying plain-sand joints clears the current weeds but does nothing to stop the next crop rooting in loose sand. If you stay with regular sand, plan on sweeping, spot weeding and an occasional treatment from our [weed killer guide](/best-weed-killer/) every season.

sections.heading: Does Polymeric Sand Stop Pavers From Draining?
sections.body:
No. Water still passes through and around cured polymeric joints into the bedding layer, just more slowly than through loose sand. Most patios are built to shed the bulk of their rain across the surface toward the edges anyway, so the practical difference is small.

### Permeable pavers are the exception

Permeable paver systems are built with wider joints filled with open-graded chip stone so water drains straight through into a deep stone reservoir. Neither regular sand nor polymeric sand belongs in those joints; both would clog them and can conflict with local stormwater rules. Use the aggregate the paver maker specifies. If your joints are noticeably wide and filled with small stones rather than sand, you probably have a permeable system.

### Movement is the bigger difference

Regular sand moves with the pavers. A patio that settles or heaves a little each year just reshuffles its joints, and you sweep in more sand. Polymeric sand is firmer, so a moving base cracks it. On a sound base, that is not a problem. On a failing base, polymeric sand will reveal the movement quickly.

### Climate

In deep-frost regions, a well-built base keeps movement small and polymeric joints hold up fine. On expansive clay soils that swell and shrink with moisture, even good bases can shift a little, and a slightly flexible gel-type polymeric sand or plain sand copes better than the firmest formulas.

sections.heading: Which Is Easier to Install?
sections.body:
Regular sand, by a wide margin.

### Regular sand

Sweep it in, compact, sweep in more and hose off the surface. Weather barely matters, the pavers can be damp and mistakes are fixed by sweeping in another bag. There is no haze risk and no cure time.

### Polymeric sand

The pavers and joints must be completely dry, the forecast clear for a day or two, and every grain swept and blown off the faces before watering. The watering itself is a controlled series of light passes. Over-watering or rain too soon can leave haze on the pavers or soft joints that have to be dug out. None of it is beyond a careful homeowner, and our [how to use polymeric sand guide](/how-to-use-polymeric-sand/) lays out every step, but you do have to pick your day and resist rushing.

### Same tools either way

Both need compaction to settle the sand to the bottom of the joints, which on anything larger than a small landing means renting a plate compactor with a protective pad. That cost is identical, so it should not sway the decision.

### Timing is the hidden cost

Regular sand can go in on any afternoon, even right after a shower. Polymeric sand may mean waiting a week or more in a wet spring for two clear days in a row. If you need the patio usable for an event, plain sand gets you there now, and you can upgrade the joints in the next dry spell.

sections.heading: Polymeric Sand vs Regular Sand: Which Costs Less Over Five Years?
sections.body:
Regular sand costs less on day one. Over five years, the gap narrows, and the time saved usually tips the balance toward polymeric sand.

### A 300 square foot patio of 4 x 8 inch pavers

Either product typically takes three to five bags for a patio this size; small pavers and wider joints use more. At typical home-center prices, the initial fill with regular sand is a small expense, while polymeric sand usually adds somewhere around $70 to $210 in material.

### Upkeep

Regular sand usually needs topping up every year or two plus weed control, so you keep buying a bag or two and some weed killer. Polymeric sand installed well usually needs only sweeping until its first refresh, 3 to 10 years out.

### Time

This is the bigger difference. Regular sand means a few hours a year sweeping sand in and pulling weeds. Polymeric sand means one careful weekend and then little attention for years. Most people who switch say the time saved matters more than the money.

### Where polymeric gets expensive

Wide-joint natural stone can use a bag every 10 to 20 square feet, so flagstone patios cost far more to fill with a polymeric binder. Price that out before committing. For the full ledger beyond cost, read our [polymeric sand pros and cons](/polymeric-sand-pros-and-cons/).

sections.heading: When Is Regular Sand the Better Choice?
sections.body:
There are real cases where plain sand is the right call.

### The base still moves

If pavers shift every winter and you are not ready to rebuild the base, regular sand moves with them while polymeric sand would crack. Fix the base later and switch then.

### Temporary or casual surfaces

A path you might move, a rental property patio or a garden area where a few weeds do not bother you does not need the long-term benefit. Low cost and easy installation win.

### Haze is unacceptable and conditions are poor

On very porous or light-colored stone in a climate with few dry spells, regular sand removes the haze risk entirely, at the price of more maintenance.

### Polymeric sand vs mortar

Mortar belongs on pavers and stone set on a rigid concrete slab, where joints are often too shallow for polymeric sand. On a flexible gravel base, mortar cracks as the pavers flex, so for a standard sand-set patio the real choice is between polymeric and regular sand, not mortar. If you do have mortar joints, a [grout sealer](/best-grout-sealer/) helps them resist water and stains.

### Permeable pavers use neither

They need clean chip stone in the joints. Ask the installer if you are unsure which system you have.

sections.heading: How Do You Switch From Regular Sand to Polymeric Sand?
sections.body:
You cannot sweep polymeric sand over the old regular sand. The binder needs at least 1 to 1.5 inches of depth, and a thin layer over loose sand cracks and lifts quickly. The old sand comes out first.

### Clear the joints

A pressure washer with a turbo or narrow tip, held low and run along the joints, is the fastest way. Do not blast out the bedding sand under the paver edges. On small areas, a joint-cleaning tool or stiff wire brush works. Pull weeds by the roots, and clean oil and rust from the faces while the joints are open; our [driveway cleaner guide](/best-driveway-cleaner/) covers the usual stains.

### Fix and dry

Re-bed any paver that rocks after cleaning. Then let everything dry completely, often two to three dry days after pressure washing and longer in shade or humidity. The joints must be dry to the bottom.

### Install and protect

Sweep in, compact, refill, clean the faces and water in light passes, exactly as on a new patio. Once the sand has fully cured, sealing the pavers with a product from our [paver sealer roundup](/best-paver-sealer/) helps the new joints shed water and last longer.

mistakes.title: Using play sand or mason sand in joints
mistakes.body: Both are fine and rounded, so they never lock together and wash out after a few storms. If you choose regular sand, buy a sharp, angular product such as kiln-dried paver joint sand or dry concrete sand. The small extra cost pays back in firmer joints and fewer top-ups.

mistakes.title: Sweeping polymeric sand over old regular sand
mistakes.body: A thin polymeric cap over loose sand cracks and lifts within a season because the binder needs 1 to 1.5 inches of depth. Clear the old sand to that depth with a pressure washer or joint tool, let the joints dry fully, then install the polymeric sand.

mistakes.title: Choosing polymeric sand for a moving base
mistakes.body: Firm polymeric joints crack when pavers settle or heave each winter. If the base is failing and you cannot fix it yet, regular sand is the more forgiving short-term choice. Pavers that rock underfoot are the warning sign; rebuild the base before upgrading the joints.

mistakes.title: Expecting polymeric sand to end all weeding
mistakes.body: It sharply reduces weeds rooting in the joints, but wind-blown seeds still sprout in dust and debris on top. Regular sweeping is still needed. Pulling a few shallow weeds each month is normal upkeep, not a product failure, and owners who expect zero maintenance are the ones left disappointed.

mistakes.title: Filling permeable pavers with any sand
mistakes.body: Permeable systems need open-graded chip stone in the joints so water drains straight through. Regular sand and polymeric sand both clog that system and can conflict with local stormwater requirements. Wide joints holding small stones instead of sand are the giveaway, so check before you buy.

faqs.q: Is polymeric sand better than regular sand for pavers?
faqs.a: Yes, for most concrete paver patios, walkways and driveways. Polymeric sand keeps joints full, resists weeds and ants and rarely washes out when installed properly. Regular sand is cheaper and easier but needs topping up and weeding. Regular sand is the better pick for a moving base, a temporary surface or when you cannot get the dry weather polymeric sand needs.

faqs.q: What type of sand is best for paver joints?
faqs.a: Polymeric sand is the best joint sand for most paver patios. If you want regular sand, use an angular product that packs tightly, such as kiln-dried paver joint sand or dry concrete sand, and avoid play sand and mason sand, which are fine and rounded and wash out quickly. Whatever you choose, it must be dry to sweep into narrow joints.

faqs.q: Can I mix polymeric sand with regular sand?
faqs.a: No, not as a way to save money. Blending in plain sand dilutes the binder and weakens the joint, and makers do not recommend it. Use polymeric sand straight from the bag. If budget is tight, use regular sand on less important areas and save polymeric sand for the spots where weeds and washout bother you most.

faqs.q: Is play sand the same as polymeric sand?
faqs.a: No. Play sand is plain, fine, rounded sand with no binder, while polymeric sand is graded sand mixed with a polymer that hardens when wet. Play sand is also a poor choice for paver joints in general, because the rounded grains do not lock together and wash out quickly. Use kiln-dried joint sand or polymeric sand instead.

faqs.q: How often does regular paver sand need replacing?
faqs.a: Usually every year or two, depending on rainfall, slope, traffic and how often you pressure wash. Joints that drop below the paver edge let pavers shift and invite weeds, so top them up when you see gaps. Areas near downspouts and at the bottom of slopes typically need attention first.

faqs.q: Is polymeric sand worth the cost on a small patio?
faqs.a: Usually yes. On a 100 to 150 square foot patio, the material difference is small, while polymeric sand saves yearly topping up and weeding. The bigger question is whether you can give it the dry weather and careful installation it needs. If not, regular sand is a reasonable choice, and you can upgrade later.

faqs.q: Should I use polymeric sand or mortar for paver joints?
faqs.a: Use polymeric sand for pavers laid on a compacted gravel and sand base, and mortar only for pavers or stone set on a rigid concrete slab. Mortar over a flexible base cracks as the pavers move, especially in freeze-thaw climates. Polymeric sand flexes slightly with the patio, which is why it is standard on sand-set paver work.

bottomLine: For a concrete paver patio, walkway or driveway on a sound base, polymeric sand is the better choice. It costs more up front and takes a careful, dry-weather weekend to install, but it ends the cycle of washed-out joints, weeds and ant hills that comes with plain sand, and it typically lasts 3 to 10 years before a refresh. Regular angular joint sand still makes sense on a base that moves, on temporary or casual surfaces and when you cannot get two dry days, and neither belongs in permeable pavers. If you are switching, clear the old sand to full depth, let the joints dry and follow the installation steps exactly.
